claims.text: A hybrid Bayesian approach combining targeted high-temperature experiments with computational thermodynamic models can accurately predict thermodynamic behavior across broad high-entropy-alloy composition spaces.
The hybrid approach can achieve its predictions with substantially less experimental effort than exhaustive characterization.
As-cast or homogenized multi-principal-element alloys without prior melting or solidification cycles are suitable initial states for the proposed measurements.
A small set of DSC and in situ high-temperature diffraction experiments can support iterative Bayesian updating of the model.
CALPHAD and first-principles calculations can be combined with partial thermodynamic data to refine solid- and liquid-phase free-energy descriptions.
Measurements from ambient temperature to approximately 300 K above each alloy's expected melting point provide an adequate calibration range.
Inert or vacuum environments mitigate oxidation or contamination during the high-temperature measurements.
Refined free-energy descriptions can capture composition and temperature dependencies of the solid-liquid boundary.
Bayesian inference narrows uncertainty in thermodynamic parameters by combining experimental measurements with computational predictions.
Narrowing thermodynamic-parameter uncertainty improves calculations of phase transitions and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties in high-entropy alloys.
The approach can determine melting temperatures to within ±20 K.
The approach can determine enthalpies of fusion to within ±5%.
The approach can determine entropies of fusion to within ±5%.
The approach can determine volume changes upon melting to within ±5%.
Conventional CALPHAD and first-principles approaches require larger calibration datasets, have slower throughput, and provide less robust uncertainty quantification.
The approach is primarily applicable to HEAs with limited short-range ordering and near-equimolar or moderately off-equimolar compositions.
Complex phases or extreme compositions require additional validation or more extensive experimental input.
Predictive fidelity depends on the breadth and quality of existing thermodynamic data and on the number and temperature range of calibration experiments.
DSC and in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction can independently quantify melting temperature, fusion properties, and volume change at melting for held-out alloys.
Systematic errors exceeding the uncertainty bounds, such as more than 20 K for melting temperature or more than 5% for fusion enthalpy, would invalidate the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: An as-cast alloy has necessarily undergone a melting and solidification cycle during casting, conflicting with the simultaneous requirement that it have no prior melting or solidification cycles.
